endings.text:
End of the Romanesque walk. Rough stone, round arches, towers: the fashion of the 1880s on this street.

But Richardson's fortress outlived nearly every house around it, and it is still standing. Walk back up to Eighteenth Street and look at it once more in the winter light.

evidence.text: Joseph G. Coleman Residence. Built 1886; Cobb & Frost, architects. Cobb & Frost were well known for their designs in the Romanesque style, executed here in rough-faced brown sandstone.

evidence.locator: The whole plate: the street front and south flank from the roadway south-west of the house.
evidence.text: The 1888 plate shows a rock-faced brown-stone front with a deep round arch on clustered columns over a broad stair, and a corbelled oriel over the arch.

evidence.locator: HABS transcription, data pages 13-15; construction description, not the 1923 garage conversion.
evidence.text: Glessner describes unglazed red roof tiles and granite street walls as part of the house's construction.
John Glessner Residence. Built 1887; Henry Hobson Richardson, architect. Designed in the Richardsonian Romanesque style, the house is wrapped around a spacious light-filled courtyard.
The district draft reads 2011 Prairie from the T-1837 register as Romanesque: a rough ashlar front, a round-arched entrance and a rounded corner turret under a conical cap.

The district draft reads the Harriet Rees house (Cobb & Frost, 1888) from the T-1837 register as Romanesque: a limestone front under a tall gable facing the avenue; its carved tympanum, loggia and bowed oriel are later refinements.
The route, its order, its winter afternoon, its reading times, its keepsake and its framing are modern interpretation; no historical visit, conversation or occupant on a day in 1904 is asserted.
Glessner remembered Richardson weighing three hundred and seventy pounds: 'big-minded, big-bodied, big-hearted'.
Richardson held that the windows of a city house were 'not to look out of', since people shroud them in shades and curtains.

evidence.locator: Data page 21, Part II.B.2, Wall construction.
evidence.text: The street walls are brick faced with alternately six- and eight-inch sheets of granite, with deeper slabs returned at the openings to imply a wall entirely of stone.
George Pullman, across the street, complained of the Glessner house: 'I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door'.

opening.text:
JAUNT: ROMANESQUE STYLE. A winter afternoon, 1904, the elms bare and the stone showing. In the 1880s one architect from Boston, Henry Hobson Richardson, made heavy stone fashionable again: rough-faced blocks, deep round arches like a castle gate, and towers. Chicago loved it, and for a few years its rich wanted fortresses.

Four houses on foot, 1800 to 2110 Prairie. Look for rock-faced stone, arches that seem to sink into the wall, and turrets. Two of the four are still rough first models in this reconstruction.

Start with the house that started it, the one its neighbours hated.

armour_corwith_house_1945_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Henry Corwith here. Before them, the Armour household lived here (1890-1891).

armour_house_2115_prairie.text: A stone house with a steep mansard roof, built for the lumberman David Kelley. The family of the meatpacker Philip D. Armour lived here for nearly 50 years. Armour's widow was one of the last people living on the street.

buckingham_house_2036_prairie.text: Clarence Buckingham's house in the 1904 Blue Book. In 1927 his sister Kate will give Chicago the Buckingham Fountain in his memory, its centre jet throwing water 150 feet up.

coleman_ames_house_1811_prairie.text: A Romanesque house of rough brown sandstone, built in 1886 for Joseph G. Coleman. Cobb and Frost were the architects. It still stands.

dent_house_1823_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Thomas Dent here, a lawyer by the 1900 census.

dexter_house_1721_prairie.text: Wirt Dexter's house of 1863, given a new front by Arthur Little in 1889. By 1904 the Blue Book lists Henry H. Walker here.

edson_keith_house_1906_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Edson Keith here.

elbridge_keith_house_1900_prairie.text: A limestone house with a steep slate roof, built for Elbridge Keith, a hat merchant who became a banker. The top floor inside that roof was added in the 1880s. It is the last Second Empire house left on Prairie Avenue.

fort_dearborn_massacre_monument_1893.text: A bronze group by Carl Rohl-Smith, paid for by George M. Pullman and set up beside his house in 1893. It shows the Potawatomi leader Black Partridge saving Margaret Helm during the battle of August 1812.

george_glessner_house_1706_prairie.text: Home of George M. Glessner, son of the granite house at 1800; the Glessners built it beside his sister's house at 1700.

glessner_house.text: A granite fortress on the street, with a sunny courtyard inside. People passing by remarked on its narrow windows along 18th Street, not knowing the big ones face the courtyard. By 1904 John and Frances Glessner had lived here since 1887.

glessner_lee_house_1700_prairie.text: Built by the Glessners for their daughter Frances, who married Blewett Lee in 1898. Decades on she will build the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, tiny crime scenes still used to train investigators.

goodman_house_1612_prairie.text: Joseph Goodman's stone Italianate of 1869, two years before the Great Fire: round-headed windows under long keystones, and an arched portico at the top of a high stoop.

henderson_house_1816_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Charles M. Henderson here. Before them, W. H. Merrill jr. lived here (1899-1903).

hibbard_house_1701_prairie.text: William G. Hibbard's house of 1869, by William Le Baron Jenney, who fifteen years later built the Home Insurance Building, called the first skyscraper.

high_house_2021_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. James L. High here.

house_1600_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists John G. Shortall here, a capitalist by the 1900 census.

house_1608_prairie.text: The Frank household. Henrietta Greenebaum Frank and her sister Hannah Greenebaum Solomon became the first Jewish members of the Chicago Woman's Club in 1876.

house_1616_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists William R. Stirling here.

house_1619_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Howard E. Perry here, a clerk by the 1900 census. Before them, Walter H. Wilson lived here (1891).

house_1621_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists John H. Hamline here, a lawyer by the 1900 census.

house_1625_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Hugh J. McBirney here.

house_1626_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists A. Longini here.

house_1628_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists M. Einstein here, a capitalist by the 1900 census.

house_1634_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists T. H. Bellas here, a commission merchant by the 1900 census. Before them, the Lorimer household lived here (1890-1891).

house_1636_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. H. Morris Johnston here.

house_1708_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists A. A. Carpenter jr. here. Before them, Stanley Field lived here (1902).

house_1726_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists James R. Walker here.

house_1730_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Joseph E. Otis here.

house_1736_prairie.text: A brick house with a mansard roof, on the corner of 18th Street. Its sources disagree on when it was built: 1864 or 1875. From 1880 it was the home of Hugh McBirney, who made white lead for paint.

house_1828_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Daniel B. Shipman here.

house_2000_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists John M. Clark here.

house_2003_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. H. W. Hoyt here. Before them, the Bissell household lived here (1890-1897).

house_2010_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists W. L. Grey here.

house_2011_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Augustus D. Lamb here. Before them, J. R. Dunlop lived here (1891-1892).

house_2017_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists A. J. McBean here, a cement manufacturer by the 1900 census. Before them, Mrs. William Armour lived here (1890-1893).

house_2018_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. L. A. Herrick here. Before them, Josiah L. Lombard lived here (1891-1893).

house_2026_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. D. Stettauer here. Before them, Miss Mary Norton lived here (1890-1893).

house_2027_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. J. J. Borland here. Before them, the Walker household lived here (1890-1902).

house_2101_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Eugene S. Pike here. Before them, Mrs. Helen Rockwell lived here (1891-1903).

house_2123_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Thomas H. Hulbert here. Before them, the Avery household lived here (1890-1901).

jones_house_1834_prairie.text: A brick Italianate house by John M. Van Osdel, built in 1866 for Fernando Jones, one of Chicago's earliest settlers. In 1886 it gained a mansard roof, to keep up with its neighbors.

keith_house_1808_prairie.text: Osborn R. Keith's granite-fronted house of 1886 by Cobb and Frost, noticed that year at forty thousand dollars, going up as Richardson's granite house rose next door.

kellogg_house_1709_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Jesse Spalding here, a lumberman by the 1900 census. Before them, Mrs. Palmer V. Kellogg lived here (1890-1893).

kellogg_house_1923_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. C. P. Kellogg here. Before them, Pierrepont Isham lived here (1895-1899).

kimball_house_1801_prairie.text: A house in the French château style, built in 1890 for William W. Kimball. He made pianos and organs. Solon S. Beman was the architect.

law_house_1620_prairie.text: Robert Law's house, engraved in 1874 for a series on the homes of Chicago: two storeys over a raised basement under a slated mansard.

marsh_house_1824_prairie.text: Samuel B. Pomeroy's Italianate villa of 1857, one of the oldest houses on the street, hiding behind the stone front George B. Marsh gave it after 1880.

marshall_field_house_1905_prairie.text: Marshall Field's house, by Richard Morris Hunt, the architect of the Statue of Liberty's pedestal. Field is the wealthiest businessman in Chicago, and the street's most famous neighbour.

marshall_field_jr_house_1919_prairie.text: Built in 1867 and made bigger several times. Marshall Field Jr. bought it in 1890. In 1902 D. H. Burnham and Company added a huge new part.

mayer_house_2009_prairie.text: Max A. Meyer's house of 1888, a French Gothic rowhouse by Burnham and Root.

moulton_lowden_house_1912_prairie.text: A big house in the French château style, built in 1882 for B. P. Moulton. In 1898 Frank O. Lowden moved in. He later became governor of Illinois.

otis_house_2033_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists F. R. Otis here.

pullman_house_1729_prairie.text: George M. Pullman's mansion, built between 1870 and 1876. Inside were a theatre for about 200 people, a pipe organ and a bowling alley.

ream_house_1901_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Norman B. Ream here, a capitalist by the 1900 census.

rees_house_2110_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Edson Keith jr. here. Before them, Mrs. James H. Rees lived here (1890-1892).

reid_house_2013_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists William H. Reid here.

robbins_house_2126_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Edward F. Robbins here. Before them, the Hamill household lived here (1890-1899).

roloson_house_2109_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Robert W. Roloson here. Before them, Mrs. Judith L. Marshall lived here (1890-1899).

rothschild_house_2112_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. M. M. Rothschild here.

sears_meeker_house_1815_prairie.text: Built for Joseph Sears; by 1904 the Blue Book lists Arthur Meeker here.

sherman_house_2100_prairie.text: Built in 1874 for John B. Sherman, who ran the Union Stock Yards. Burnham and Root were the architects. Sherman's daughter Margaret married Daniel Burnham while it was going up.

shortall_gregory_house_1638_prairie_fron.text: Built in 1868. In 1904 the Blue Book lists Robert B. Gregory here.

spalding_house_1637_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists William Gold Hibbard jr. here. Before them, the Spalding household lived here (1890-1899).

stone_house_2035_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. H. O. Stone here.

tolman_house_2031_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Samuel A. Tolman here.

tucker_smith_house_2140_prairie.text: Built in 1876. In 1904 the Blue Book lists Byron L. Smith here.

walker_house_1720_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. James M. Walker here. Before them, Miss Jennie Royce lived here (1890-1891).

wheeler_house_1812_prairie.text: A brick row house in the Dutch style, built in 1884 for George H. Wheeler. He owned grain elevators. Burnham and Root designed it.

premise: Rough-faced stone, deep round arches, turrets: four Romanesque fronts from Eighteenth Street to Twenty-first.

stops.text: 1800 Prairie, Glessner House, the street's Richardsonian Romanesque original. Its street walls are brick faced with alternate six- and eight-inch sheets of granite, cut deeper at the openings so the whole wall looks solid stone, under a roof of unglazed red tiles. Richardson, all 370 pounds of him, held that the windows of a city house were 'not to look out of', so the street side is nearly blank and the family rooms open on a courtyard behind. George Pullman, across the corner, complained about 'that thing staring me in the face'. Across the avenue and a little south, the style caught on.

1811 Prairie, the Coleman house of 1886, by Cobb and Frost, who were well known for their Romanesque work. This front is rough-faced brown sandstone. The 1888 plate shows the style's signature: a deep round arch on clustered columns over a broad stair, and a corbelled oriel bulging out above it, like a lookout on a castle wall. Notice that the arch is the door: in this style, the entrance is a tunnel into the stone. Walk south past Twentieth Street for two smaller fortresses.

2011 Prairie, a neighbour of the Mayer house. The district register reads it as Romanesque: a rough ashlar front, a round-arched entrance, and a rounded corner turret under a conical cap. A turret on a city lot is pure theatre: a castle tower on a town house. Across the avenue and a block on, the last of the four squeezes the style onto one narrow lot.

2110 Prairie, Harriet Rees's narrow house, read by the district register as Cobb and Frost's work of 1888 and as Romanesque: a limestone front under a tall gable facing the avenue. Two years after their Coleman house, the same architects did the style in pale stone for a woman's house. Compare the two: same firm, opposite colour.
